entries.title: Romare Bearden: Collage as a Language of Black Life
entries.body_text: Romare Bearden was born on September 2, 1911, in Charlotte, North Carolina, and grew up in Harlem during its cultural renaissance. A painter, cartoonist, and collagist, Bearden developed his most distinctive work during the 1960s, when he turned to photomontage and collage to build a layered visual language rooted in African American history, jazz, mythology, and memory. In 1963, alongside Norman Lewis and others, he co-founded Spiral — a collective of Black artists who gathered in New York to discuss how art could respond to the Civil Rights Movement. His series 'The Prevalence of Ritual' (1964) used cut magazine photographs, colored paper, and paint to construct dense, fragmented portraits of Black life and sacred experience across the rural South and urban North. Bearden died on March 12, 1988, leaving a body of work that remains one of the most searching investigations of community, identity, and cultural continuity in American art.

entries.title: Grandma Moses: Late Bloomer, Lifelong Observer
entries.body_text: Anna Mary Robertson Moses — known universally as Grandma Moses — was born on September 7, 1860, in Greenwich, New York. She spent most of her life farming, and did not begin painting in earnest until she was in her late 70s, after arthritis made embroidery too painful to continue. In 1938, a collector named Louis Caldor spotted her paintings in a drugstore window in Hoosick Falls, New York, and brought them to the attention of gallerist Otto Kallir, who gave her a first solo exhibition the following year. Moses painted from memory — vivid, affectionately detailed scenes of farm life, harvest seasons, sleigh rides, and maple-sugaring — with a compositional confidence and warmth that defied her lack of formal training. She appeared on the cover of TIME magazine for her 100th birthday and received the Women's National Press Club Award in 1949. She died on December 13, 1961, at the age of 101. Her story remains a powerful argument for art as a practice belonging to every stage of life.
entries.image_alt_text: The Old Oaken Bucket by Grandma Moses, 1943, oil on Masonite, depicting a snowy New England farm scene with figures drawing water from a well surrounded by bare winter trees
entries.source_name: Galerie St. Etienne, New York — Grandma Moses Archive

entries.title: El Anatsui on Material, History, and What Objects Carry
entries.body_text: These materials are not just aesthetic objects. They carry within them the weight of human history and activity.
entries.image_alt_text: Earth's Skin by El Anatsui, 2007, aluminum and copper wire, large-scale flexible wall sculpture composed of thousands of flattened bottle caps and aluminum liquor seals in warm earth tones, golds, and silvers

entries.body_text: I paint with my back to the world.

entries.title: Alma Thomas: Color, Joy, and a Garden at the Edge of History
entries.body_text: Alma Woodsey Thomas was born on September 22, 1891, in Columbus, Georgia, and grew up in Washington, D.C., where her family relocated to escape the racial violence of the post-Reconstruction South. She became the first graduate of Howard University's art department in 1924 and taught art at Shaw Junior High School in D.C. for 35 years. It was only after retirement, in her late 60s and 70s, that Thomas developed the luminous mosaic-like style for which she is now celebrated: concentric rings and vertical tessellations of pure, singing color drawn from the garden outside her D.C. home, the cross-sections of tree trunks, and the patterns she observed through her kitchen window. In 1972, she became the first Black woman to hold a solo exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art. Thomas died on February 24, 1978. Her paintings — radiant, unhurried, botanically joyful — stand as one of American abstraction's most original and long-undersung achievements.
entries.image_alt_text: Iris, Tulips, Jonquils, and Crocuses by Alma Thomas, 1969, acrylic on canvas, 152.6 x 121.9 cm, Smithsonian American Art Museum, Washington D.C.
entries.rights_note: Alma Thomas died February 24, 1978. Works are under copyright. Contact the Smithsonian American Art Museum for open-access image licensing and authorized reproduction.

entries.title: Artemisia Gentileschi on the Spirit Within the Work
entries.body_text: You will find the spirit of Caesar in this soul of a woman.
entries.image_alt_text: Judith Slaying Holofernes by Artemisia Gentileschi, c. 1614-20, oil on canvas, 199 x 162.5 cm, Uffizi Gallery, Florence
